title: The kingdom within (II.1)
hook: the kingdom of God is within you
tomorrow: can a calm person really do more good than a smart one?

segments.voice: That was a week in book one of the Imitation: resist at the start, bear with others since you have yours, a cell that grows sweet, everyone's sorrow, as if today. Yesterday's line closed it: steady zeal.

A map app can drop a pin on almost anything: a taco truck, a friend's parked car, a seat in a stadium. In Luke's Gospel, some Pharisees ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come, and he won't give them a pin. It doesn't come in a way you can watch for, he says, and nobody will say look here, or look there. Not a building, not a border, not a date. Then comes the line the Imitation picks up to open book two.
screen: `A PIN ON THE MAP.` → `WHEN WILL THE KINGDOM COME?` → `NOT HERE, NOT THERE.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "For lo, the kingdom of God is within you." The Imitation starts book two right there. Turn to the Lord with your whole heart, it says, hold outward things more lightly, and you'll see the kingdom of God come within you. Some readers hear Luke's little word within as inside you. Some hear among you, Jesus standing right there in the crowd. The Imitation leans on inside. Then a picture. Christ often visits the inward person, the chapter says, and the visit brings sweet conversation, comfort, much peace, and a closeness it calls wonderful. A house with a guest. And a warning that keeps it honest: don't lean your whole weight on people, even good and dear ones, because people change. Not because they're worthless. Because the floor that holds is further in. Now look back at the week, because it was building to this door. Resisting at the start was guarding the entrance. Bearing with others was making room. The cell was the quiet room itself. Everyone's sorrow and as if today cleared out false hopes and later-maybe plans. Steady zeal kept the place swept. Book one was housekeeping. Book two opens the inner door, and says someone is already on the way.
screen: `WITHIN YOU, OR AMONG YOU.` · `CHRIST VISITS THE INWARD PERSON.` · `THE FLOOR THAT HOLDS IS FURTHER IN.` · `BOOK ONE SWEPT THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and come inward in three steps: the sounds in the room, then your breath, then the quiet underneath it. Three steps, no hurry. When a thought pulls you back outside, turn in again, gently, without scolding yourself. If you pray, you can rest on Luke's line: the kingdom of God is within you.
The kingdom within. Jesus's line in Luke, and the first words of book two of the Imitation: God's reign, found by turning inward.
The line to keep: within you, not over here and not over there. A week ends on a quiet door.

howItsDone: Catholics read the Imitation of Christ as a book of spiritual reading, often a chapter at a time, and many pair it with quiet prayer, an examination of conscience or time before the Blessed Sacrament.

notes: Luke 17:21 quoted from the Douay-Rheims (Challoner): 'For lo, the kingdom of God is within you.' Confirm wording. Luke 17:20–21a (not coming with observation; no one will say lo here, lo there) is paraphrased.

Imitation II.1 paraphrased: turn to the Lord with your whole heart; learn to despise outward things and give yourself to the inward, and you will see the kingdom of God come in you; Christ often visits the inward man with sweet conversation, pleasing comfort, much peace and wonderful familiarity; do not trust overmuch in a mortal man, for men change. 'Hold outward things more lightly' softens the Latin 'contemnere'; confirm the softening is fair.
The within/among reading of Luke 17:21 is offered only as 'some readers'. Pharisees appear only as the questioners in Luke 17:20, not as a foil.
